Intermittent Microaeration Enhanced Anaerobic Digestion: The Key
Role of Fe(III)/Fe(II) Cycle and Reactive Oxygen Species
Xuepeng Wang, Jinshuo Zhang, Bowen Yang, Haohao Mao, Qilin Yu, and Yaobin Zhang*
Cite This: Environ. Sci. Technol. 2025, 59, 8629−8639
Read Online

ABSTRACT: Microaeration has been reported to improve anaerobic digestion, which is generally attributed to increased microbial
diversity, but a thorough explanation is lacking. In this study, it was found that intermittent microaeration (IMA) supplied to an
anaerobic digester could oxidize Fe(II) produced by dissimilatory iron reduction (DIR) to form a Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle and generate
extracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) to improve anaerobic treatment of phenol-containing wastewater. The results showed
that compared to the control group without IMA, the removal rates of COD and phenol increased by 29.54 and 49.68 percentage
points, respectively, and daily average methane production increased by 85.44%. The Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle slowed down the loss of
iron (13.97%) released from sludge due to the lower solubility of Fe(III) and facilitated •OH generation (1.22 ± 0.04 μM) via
Fenton-like reactions. The DIR and the generation of •OH accelerated phenol degradation. Metagenomic analysis revealed that the
abundance of methanogens and antioxidant enzymes-encoding genes in response to oxidative stress significantly increased in the
IMA group compared to the control, enabling methanogenesis to proceed smoothly under microaeration. This study investigated the
extracellular ROS generation induced by microaeration during anaerobic digestion and their roles in promoting anaerobic
performance, thereby providing a new perspective for optimizing anaerobic systems with microaeration.
KEYWORDS: dissimilatory iron reduction, Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle, reactive oxygen species, antioxidant defense,
direct interspecies electron transfer
1. INTRODUCTION
Anaerobic digestion is considered one of the most widely used
technologies to treat high-concentration organic wastewater
due to its effectiveness in recovering biomass energy
(methane) from organic matter.1,2 However, anaerobic
digestion is challenged by low operational stability and slow
hydrolytic acidification of complex substrates. Additionally,
numerous toxic organic pollutants, such as phenol in industrial
organic wastewater, impede anaerobic digestion and methane
production.3,4 Phenol is widely present in industrial wastewater
from coal chemical processing, pharmaceutical manufacturing,
and other industries, and has been listed as one of the priority
control pollutants by the United States Environmental
Protection Agency due to its high toxicity.5 It has been
reported that phenol over 2000 mg/L inhibits biological
processes including anaerobic digestion due to the toxic
accumulation of phenol.6,7 Consequently, accelerating the
decomposition of phenol is essential for improving the
anaerobic treatment of phenol-containing wastewater.
The addition of iron (hydro)oxides has been extensively
reported to promote the degradation of complex organic
matter through microbially dissimilatory iron reduction
(DIR).8,9 It also can facilitate the syntrophic metabolism
between dissimilatory iron-reducing bacteria and methanogens
capable of direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) to
increase methane production.3,10 DIR, also known as iron

tion of iron (hydro)oxides to sustain a continuous DIR, which
is impractical in practice. If the Fe(II) produced by DIR in the
anaerobic process can be oxidized to Fe(III) to drive an
Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle, then this iron-based method relying on
DIR is expected to be applied in practical engineering.
Many oxidants, such as O2 and NO2
−/NO3
−, can oxidize
Fe(II), resulting in the widespread occurrence of the Fe(III)/
Fe(II) cycle in natural water systems.11,12 Notably, O2, as the
most ubiquitous oxidant, can microbially oxidize Fe(II) by
neutrophilic Fe(II)-oxidizing bacteria, which grow autotroph-

electron acceptor (reaction 1):12

On the other hand, from a traditional perspective, O2 should
be avoided as much as possible during anaerobic digestion to
minimize its negative effects on obligate anaerobic micro-
organisms.13 Nevertheless, recent studies have reported that
microaeration can promote anaerobic digestion.13,14 This
might be attributed to the fact that microaeration enhances
microbial diversity, which is beneficial for the hydrolysis of
complex organic matter and the removal of hydrogen
sulfide.15−17 Also, the stirring effect of intermittent microaera-
tion increases mass transfer.18,19 However, it remains unclear
whether the Fe(II) oxidation and ROS generation are involved
in the promotion of anaerobic methanogenesis by intermittent
microaeration.
Theoretically, intermittent microaeration is capable of
reoxidizing Fe(II) to Fe(III) in anaerobic digestion systems,
thereby driving the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle and creating a
continuous DIR.20,21 In this process, the generated ROS
together with the Fe(II) oxidation are likely to attack the
macromolecular organic matter,22,23 and the sustained DIR
caused by Fe(III) generation may accelerate the decom-
position of the organic matter for methane production. In
previous studies, intermittent aeration-driven Fe(III)/Fe(II)
has been shown to promote anaerobic ammonium removal and
persistent organic pollutant degradation.20,24
Several studies have reported ROS generation in anaerobic
digesters.25−27 However, most of these studies focus only on its
adverse effects. That is to say, under unfavorable metabolic
conditions, the accumulation of intracellular ROS may
suppress metabolic activities, which in turn leads to the
deterioration of the performance of anaerobic digesters.28,29
For instance, Wei et al. documented the generation of
intracellular ROS triggered by microplastics during the
anaerobic digestion of waste-activated sludge, which signifi-
cantly inhibited the digestion process.26 This discrepancy
hinders a more in-depth understanding of how the ROS
induced by intermittent microaeration affects microbial
processes. The impacts of ROS induced by intermittent
microaeration on methanogenesis and anaerobic microbial
metabolism remain ambiguous.
This study aimed to identify and validate the Fe(III)/Fe(II)
cycle and ROS induced by intermittent microaeration during
anaerobic methanogenesis. Furthermore, the influence of
intermittent microaeration on the evolution of the microbial
community was investigated.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Inoculum Sludge and Ferrihydrite Preparation.
The inoculum sludge was collected from the anaerobic tank of
a municipal sludge treatment plant in Dalian, China, with a
total solids (TSS) concentration of 39.75 g/L and volatile
solids (VSS) of 36.65 g/L. Ferrihydrite was synthesized by
neutralizing a 50 mM FeCl3 solution with 0.5 M NaOH to a
pH of about 7, as reported previously.30 The morphology of
the synthesized ferrihydrite is shown in Figure S1.
2.2. Operation of Reactors. Two parallel continuous-flow
UASB reactors (φ70 mm × 300 mm, working volume: 1000
mL) were used for the anaerobic digestion. Each reactor was
inoculated with 300 mL inoculum sludge and 700 mL of
synthesized wastewater as the feeding substances. Besides, each
reactor received the synthesized ferrihydrite with a final Fe(III)
concentration of 15 mM. The initial composition of the
synthesized wastewater (per liter) was as follows: 2.50 g
glucose, 0.23 g NH4Cl, 0.05 g KH2PO4, 2.50 g NaHCO3, and
10 mL trace elements.31 The hydraulic retention time was
controlled at 30 h, and the reactor was operated at 33 ± 1 °C.
One reactor received intermittent microaeration (referred to as
the intermittent microaeration group, IMA group), with an
aeration intensity of 14 mL O2/(Lreactor·day), and the aeration
was carried out for 30 min every 3 h. The other reactor served
as a control (Control group) and was supplied with N2
according to the same aeration schedule as that of the IMA
group. The selection of ferrihydrite dosing and the intensity/
frequency of microaeration are detailed in Text S1.
The continuous-flow experiments were carried out for 124
days. During the first 40 days, glucose was used as the sole
carbon source, and the influent COD gradually increased from
2500 to 8000 mg/L. After that, glucose was gradually replaced
by phenol as the substrate. The detailed variation of influent
substrate during the operation is presented in Table S1.
2.3. ROS Measurement. The generation of
•OH was
determined by an electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)
spectrometer and quantified using coumarin, as described in
Text S2. The •OH generation pathways were investigated by
examining its intermediates (e.g., •O2
−and H2O2). To verify
the pathway of •OH generation, various ROS scavengers were
added separately to the digester. Nitro blue tetrazolium (NBT)
(5 mM) was employed to scavenge •O2
−, and catalase (CAT)
(1000 U/mL) was used to scavenge H2O2. Additionally, tert-
butanol (TBA) and n-butanol (NBA) were utilized as •OH
quenchers.23,32
2.4. Characterization and Analysis. The morphology of
the synthesized ferrihydrite was characterized by means of a
scanning electron microscope and X-ray diffraction. The

The effluent from the anaerobic reactors was analyzed every
2 days. TSS, VSS, COD, the total content of ferrous and ferric
iron, as well as the content and volume of biogas were analyzed
as previously reported.34,35 The phenol concentration was
quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (Shi-
madzu, LC-2050C, Japan) with a C18 column (5 μm, 250 μm
× 4.6 mm). The mobile phase, with a flow rate of 1 mL/min,
was the mixture of methanol and H2O (70:30, V/V).
The detailed methods for characterization and analysis are
described in Text S3.
2.5. Metagenomic Analysis. After the experiments, 2 mL
of sludge samples were collected from each reactor and
subjected to metagenomic analysis by Sangon Biotech
(Shanghai) Co., Ltd., China. The detailed procedures are
described in Text S4.
2.6. Statistical Analysis. Data were expressed as mean ±
standard deviation and derived from three replicate measure-
ments. An ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) test was carried out
using R version 4.3.2 to evaluate the significance of the
differences. All the statistical differences were deemed
significant at p < 0.05.
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Performances of Methanogenic Digesters. In the
first 40 days, glucose was used as the sole substrate, and the
influent COD was gradually increased from 2500 to 8000 mg/
L. During this stage, the COD removal rate of the IMA group
was slightly higher than that of the control group, yet there was
no significant difference (Figure 1 A,B and Table S1). From
day 41 to day 70, phenol was added to the influent, and its
concentration was increased from 500 mg/L (41−58 days) to
1000 mg/L (59−70 days). The average COD concentration in
the effluent of the IMA group was 985.70 mg/L, with a
removal rate of 87.68%, which was comparable to that of the
control group (average effluent COD concentration: 972.92
mg/L, COD removal rate: 87.84%). From day 71 to day124,
when the phenol concentration increased to 2000 mg/L, the
average effluent COD concentration of the IMA group rose to
1423.62 mg/L, with a removal rate of 82.20%, which was
significantly higher than that of the control group (68.57%,
average effluent COD concentration: 2514.19 mg/L).
Specifically, during the period from 104 to day 124, the
COD removal rate of the IMA group was 84.38%, 29.54
percentage points higher than that of the control group
(54.84%).
Similarly, when the influent phenol concentration was 500
and 1000 mg/L, both groups demonstrated high phenol
removal capabilities. The phenol concentration in the effluent
was below 200 mg/L, with a removal rate of over 80%. As the
phenol concentration increased to 2000 mg/L, the average
phenol concentration in the effluent of the IMA group
increased to 531.45 mg/L, which was significantly lower than
that of the control group (1008.59 mg/L). Specifically, from
day 104 to day 124, the average phenol concentration in the

IMA group was 433.73 mg/L, much lower than that in the
control group (1427.28 mg/L). Accordingly, the phenol
removal rate of the IMA group was 49.68 percentage points
higher than that of the control group (78.31 vs 28.64%)
(Figure 1 C and Table S1).
The methanogenic capacity of the IMA group was enhanced
by intermittent microaeration (Figure 1 D and Table S1).
From day 71 to day 124, the average daily methane production
of the IMA group was 29.90% higher than that of the control
group (1.60 L/(Lreactor·d) vs 1.23 L/(Lreactor·d)). In particular,
during the period from day 104 to day 124, the average daily
methane production of the IMA group was 1.53 L/(Lreactor·d),
which was 85.44% higher than that of the control group (0.83
L/(Lreactor·d)). This might be because intermittent microaera-
tion effectively promoted the degradation of complex
substrates, providing suitable substrates for methanogens.16
Furthermore, in the last 20 days of operation, the methane
production per unit COD of the IMA group was 283.34 mL/g
COD (1530.2 mL/(8.0 g COD × 84.38% × (24/30)), which
was 13.93% higher than that of the control group (248.71 mL/
g COD). It indicated that the IMA group had a higher
methane conversion efficiency.
3.2. Role of Fe(III)/Fe(II) Cycling and ROS Generation
in Phenol Degradation. To verify whether intermittent
microaeration drives the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle, the iron
contents in the effluent and the bulk phases were determined.
As shown in Figure 2A, during the first 40 days of operation,
the average Fe(II) concentration in the effluent of the IMA
group (0.88 ± 0.31 mg/L) was 16.97% lower than that of the
control group (1.06 ± 0.47 mg/L). Moreover, the results
showed that the total iron concentration (Fe(II) + Fe(III)) in
the bulk phase of the IMA group was 550.20 ± 6.99 mg/L,
which represented a 13.97% increase compared to the control
group (482.78 ± 18.91 mg/L). The total Fe(II) and total

Fe(III) showed the same trend (Figure 2B). This elevation was
likely attributed to the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle driven by
microaeration.36,37 Considering that the ferrihydrite was only
added at the beginning of the operation, the Fe(II) produced
from the DIR might be released to the effluent, reducing the
iron content because of the higher solubility of Fe(II) under
circumneutral conditions. The lower Fe(II) contents in the
effluent and the higher iron content in the sludge of the IMA
group indicated that the oxidation of Fe(II) occurred with
intermittent microaeration.
To verify this, 1 L of the supernatant was collected from the
effluent, and 15 mM Fe(OH)2 was added. When the depletion
of organic matter failed to provide adequate electrons for DIR,
intermittent microaeration was initiated under the same
conditions as those in the above continuous flow experiment,
and the oxidation rate of Fe(II) was determined. The results
showed that intermittent microaeration could effectively
oxidize Fe(II), and an average of 1.86 mM of Fe(II) was
oxidized every 24 h, accompanied by the formation of Fe(III)
(Figure 2C). The formation of Fe(III) reduced the loss of iron
because its solubility was lower than that of Fe(II).
Furthermore, the oxidation of Fe(II) led to a continuous
supply of Fe(III), which drove DIR to degrade organic matter
and enrich iron-reducing bacteria. Iron-reducing bacteria could
obtain energy by reducing Fe(III), thus enhancing the
degradation of organic matter.38 Lovley et al. have demon-
strated that glucose fermentation combined with Fe(III)
reduction (−76 kJ/mol) was energetically more favorable
than without the reduction of Fe(III) (−71 kJ/mol).39
In addition to the function of DIR, the oxidation of Fe(II)
may induce the Haber-Weiss mechanism (reactions 2−5) to
generate ROS such as
•O2
−, H2O2, and
•OH for the
degradation of substrate (Figure 3A). During the oxidation
of Fe(II), •O2
−and H2O2 are important intermediate species,
and H2O2 is also a precursor for the production of •OH
through the Fenton-like reaction.32 The •O2
−was detected by
EPR with 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) as a
trapping agent. As shown in Figure 3B, the IMA group
exhibited a typical DMPO/•O2
−hexagonal peak (with a peak
intensity ratio of 1:1:1:1, αN = 13.36 G, αH
β = 14.06 G),40
while the control group did not show a similar peak.
Furthermore, the amount of H2O2 generated after the
microaeration was determined spectrophotometrically using
cerium sulfate. The results showed that the average
concentration of H2O2 in the IMA group was 15.54 ± 2.31
μM, whereas it was almost undetectable in the control group
(Figure 3C).
DMPO was used as a trapping agent to identify •OH. As
depicted in Figure 3B, a characteristic signal of the
DMPO/•OH complex (with a peak intensity ratio of 1:2:2:1,
αN = 14.89 G, αH
β = 14.89 G) was detected in the mud-water
mixture of the IMA group, while this characteristic peak was
absent in the control group. To determine the concentration of
•OH, 50 μM coumarin was added to the influent to capture the
• OH in situ, leading to the generation of 7-hydroxycoumar-
in.32,41 The results showed that there was a stable generation of
•OH in the IMA group (1.22 ± 0.04 μM), whereas almost no
•OH was detected in the control group during the consecutive
four-day monitoring period. To verify the generation of •OH,
alcohols (TBA and NBA) were used as •OH quenchers, and
both of them exhibited significant quenching effects on •OH
formation (Figure S2).
Furthermore, the generation pathway of
•OH was
determined through quenching experiments using NBT and
CAT. NBT acts as an efficient scavenger of •O2
−, while CAT
can decompose H2O2, thereby suppressing
•OH genera-
tion.32,42 Both NBT and CAT exhibited a significantly
inhibitory effect on the production of
•OH (Figure S2).
These results suggested that
•O2
−and H2O2 served as
intermediates in the production of •OH, and the production
pathway of
•OH was through the successive reduction of
molecular O2 (O2 →•O2
−→H2O2 →•OH) (Figure 3A).23
H2O2 and •OH were detected during anaerobic digestion,
indicating that intermittent microaeration could induce the
generation of ROS through a Fenton-like reaction.23,43 This
might be an important reason for the rapid degradation of
phenol in the IMA group.44
The degradation of phenol facilitated by DIR, in which iron-
reducing bacteria use Fe(III) oxides as the final electron
acceptors for phenol oxidation, has been proven to be an
efficient method for enhancing its anaerobic biodegrada-
tion.3,45 Besides, DIR can facilitate hydrolytic acidification
and utilize simple substrates like glucose.31 Since both the IMA
group and the control group were initially dosed with
ferrihydrite (15 mM Fe(III)), the degradation of glucose and
phenol in the two reactors was initially effective, and the
methane production was similar. However, when the phenol
concentration increased to 2000 mg/L, the control group was
unable to efficiently metabolize phenol and tended to collapse,
while the IMA group was still able to maintain a phenol
removal rate of 78.31% and stable methane production. This
might be attributed to the introduction of microaeration,
which drove the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle and generated ROS to
accelerate the degradation of phenol.
To further verify the effects of DIR and ROS generation on
phenol degradation, another experiment was carried out with
four groups using phenol (350 mg/L) as the sole carbon
source: Group A without ferrihydrite addition and microaera-
tion, Group B with ferrihydrite addition, Group C with
ferrihydrite addition and microaeration, and Group D with
ferrihydrite addition and microaeration, and formate (5 mM)
as •OH quencher (D group). The amounts of ferrihydrite
added (15 mM Fe(III)) and the microaeration pattern (14 mL
O2/(Lreactor·day)) were the same as the UASB digester.
The results showed that both ferrihydrite addition and
microaeration contributed to phenol degradation (Figure S3).
For example, on the sixth day of the reaction, the highest
removal rate of phenol was 65.41% in Group C, which was
higher than that in Group B (42.63%) and Group A (38.15%).
The difference between Group A and Group B might be due to
the effect of DIR, where phenol degradation was accompanied
by a large amount of Fe(II) production (Figure S3B).3 The
contribution of DIR to promoting phenol degradation
accounted for approximately 23.41% ((42.63−38.15%)/
(65.41−38.15%)). After adding formate as the •OH quencher,
the phenol degradation rate in Group D was 61.51%, lower
than that in Group C (65.41%). It indicated that •OH played a
role in phenol degradation, accounting for about 14.31%
((65.41−61.51%)/(65.41−38.15%)) of the increased phenol
degradation.
The degradation of phenol proceeds through different
processes depending on aerobic or anaerobic conditions.
Under aerobic conditions, phenol is decomposed into acetic
acid and succinic acid, which are subsequently mineralized into
CO2 and H2O via the tricarboxylic acid cycle. In anaerobic

main reason for the enhanced phenol degradation.48 In this

used for COD removal, it could only increase the COD
removal by 40 mg/L (14 mL × 0.001429 g/mL (SATP) × 2),
which only accounted for 1.7% of the observed increase in
phenol removal (2365 mg/L COD = (1566.27−572.72 mg/L)
× 2.34). This is because the ROS generated from the reduction
of O2 likely participated in the ring-cleavage degradation of
phenol molecules, producing intermediates that can be utilized
for methanogenesis.
3.3. Microbial Community Composition of Sludge.
The sludge collected from the reactors after 124 days of
operation was analyzed through Metagenomic analysis. There
was a distinct separation of the microbial communities
between the IMA group and the control group (Figure S4).
Intermittent microaeration enriched dissimilatory iron-reduc-
ing bacteria (Figure 4A). The abundance of dissimilatory iron-
reducing bacteria (Anaerolinea, Desulfomicrobium, Desulfovibrio,
Geobacter, Longilinea, Petrimonas, and Syntrophus) in the IMA
group (2.77%) was 1.94 times higher than that in the control
group (1.43%) (p < 0.01).49,50 Syntrophus was the predom-
inant dissimilatory iron-reducing bacteria, which was signifi-
cantly enriched in the IMA group with a relative abundance of
1.56%, much higher than the control group (0.60%) (p <
0.01). Besides, compared with the control group, Anaerolinea
(0.29 vs 0.10%, p < 0.01) and Desulfovibrio (0.27 vs 0.12%, p <
0.01) were also significantly enriched in the IMA group.
Desulfovibrio, a sulfate-reducing bacterium, can transfer
extracellular electrons to electrodes to generate electricity
and is one of the crucial electroactive bacteria involved in
DIET.49 Isolated Desulfovibrio strains could grow through
DIET when cocultured with Methanothrix harundinacea and
Methanobacterium strain YSL.51 On the other hand, Desulfovi-
brio can highly express the genes encoding cytochrome c
(CYC)-like proteins. The results of metagenomic analysis
showed that the genes encoding cytochrome c (CYC)-like
proteins in the IMA group were 1.50 times that in the control
group (Table S2) (p < 0.01).49,52
Furthermore, the expressions of other genes related to DIR,
including metal-reducing conduit biosynthesis gene cluster
mtrCAB and flavin biosynthesis gene cluster ribDCBAE were
analyzed.53 MtrA, MtrB, and MtrC form a trans-outer
membrane protein complex that mediates electron transfer
from periplasmic proteins to the bacterial surface, enabling
extracellular electron transfer (EET) through direct interaction
with external electron acceptors.54 Besides, redox-active
electron shuttles, such as flavins, are well-established mediators
of EET during microbial respiration, and an increase in their
concentration can significantly enhance the EET rates.53,55 The
results showed that the genes related to mtrCAB cluster (0.29

3.4. Enhancement of Electrochemical Activity. The
electroactivity of the microbial community was significantly
enhanced under intermittent microaeration conditions. The
curve of cyclic voltammetry (Figure 5A) showed that the
capacitance of the sludge in the IMA group was 1.60 × 10−3 F,
which was 48.14% higher than that of the sludge in the control

storage sites were involved in the electron exchange between
microorganisms and extracellular electron acceptors.3,31
In addition, the results of electrochemical impedance
spectroscopy showed that the resistance of sludge in the
IMA group was 11.11 Ω, 40.39% lower than that of the sludge

resistance suggested an increased rate of electron transfer
within the sludge. Resistance and capacitance are frequently
used as indicators to evaluate the extracellular respiration
activities of microbial communities.31,34 The lower resistance
and higher capacitance suggested that intermittent microaera-
tion improved the electroactivity of the microbial community
and facilitated extracellular electron transfer. This might be
attributed to the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle, which was beneficial for
the enrichment of electroactive microorganisms.

During anaerobic digestion, electron acceptors (such as the
reduction of H+ to H2) are necessary for acidogenic bacteria to
break down complex organic substrates. Additionally, metha-
nogens rely on the continuous utilization of the small molecule
acids and H2 generated by acidogenic bacteria to keep the pH
within a suitable range, which is essential for the continuous
decomposition of organic substances.58 Methanogens act as
the ultimate electron acceptors in the degradation of organic
matter during the metabolic exchange between acid-producing
bacteria and methanogens.59 The Fe(III) generated by
intermittent microaeration could replace methanogens as an
extracellular electron acceptor for acidogenic bacteria,
constantly facilitating extracellular respiration and ATP
synthesis.38 This could explain the improved removal of
COD facilitated by the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle.
To evaluate the methanogenic capacity of methanogens, the
abundance of genes encoding key enzymes involved in four
methanogenic pathways, namely carbon dioxide reduction
[M00567], acetate decarboxylation [M00357], methanol
methanogenesis [M00356], and methylamine/dimethyl-
amine/trimethylamine-type methanogenesis [M00563], was
analyzed based on the metagenome (Figure 6B and Table
S4).56 Among these, the reduction of carbon dioxide and the
decarboxylation of acetate were the dominant methanogenic
pathways, while the abundance of genes encoding key enzymes
for the other two methanogenic pathways was relatively low.
The genes responsible for encoding the key enzymes
involved in carbon dioxide reduction were significantly more
abundant in the IMA group (0.87) than in the control group
(0.63) (p < 0.05). Additionally, the genes encoding the key
enzymes for acetate decarboxylation in the IMA group (0.49)
were notably increased, being 1.36 times as prevalent as those
in the control group (0.36). In addition, the abundance of
genes encoding the first two enzymes of the carbon dioxide
reduction pathway, including those encoding formyl-meth-
anofuran dehydrogenase (fwdA, fwdB, fwdC, fwdD, and fwdE)
and 4Fe-4S ferric ferredoxin (fwdF and fwdG) (0.53), was
significantly higher than that of the gene encoding first enzyme
in the acetate decarboxylation pathway (acetyl-CoA decarbox-
ylase/coenzyme, 0.38) in the IMA group (p < 0.05). This
suggested that the related methanogens (i.e., Methanothrix)
might be actively engaged in reducing CO2 to CH4, i.e.,
Methanothrix produced methane through DIET.56
During the process of biological consumption, molecular O2
accepts electrons to generate •O2
−, along with H2O2 and •OH,
which can be harmful to microorganisms. Aerobic bacteria
generally possess antioxidant defense mechanisms that
counteract and alleviate the detrimental effects caused by an
overload of ROS by producing a range of antioxidant
enzymes.13 It is well-known that obligate anaerobes lack such
a defense system and are unable to survive under oxidative
stress. Recent studies have shown that some methanogenic
genera, such as Methanosarcina and Methanocella can cope with
oxidative stress by encoding a variety of antioxidant enzymes
(such as superoxide dismutase, superoxide reductase, catalases,
peroxidases, peroxiredoxins, and rubrerythrin) for detoxifica-
tion purposes.13 The results of microbial community analysis
showed that the abundances of Methanosarcina and Meth-
anocella in the IMA group were 1.38 and 1.23 times those in
the control group, respectively.
Furthermore, it has been reported that Methanothrix can
gradually establish O2 tolerance in a microaerobic environment
at an appropriate aeration intensity.60,61 However, there is
limited information available regarding its O2 tolerance
mechanisms and changes in the activities of related enzymes.
In this study, Methanothrix was enriched and became dominant
in the IMA group under an aeration intensity of 14 mL O2/
(Lreactor·day), indicating that this aeration level was within its
tolerable range. In addition, the metagenome results showed
that the levels of superoxide dismutase (EC 1.15.1.1: 0.06 vs
0.03), catalases (EC 1.11.1.6: 0.14 vs 0.12), peroxiredoxins
(EC 1.11.1.15: 0.23 vs 0.20), and catalase-peroxidase (EC
1.11.1.21: 0.13 vs 0.08) were higher in IMA groups than in the
control group (Figure 6C and Table S5). Among them, genes
encoding superoxide dismutase and peroxiredoxins are mainly
originated from Methanothrix. This indicated that Methanothrix
could effectively scavenge intracellular
•O2
−and H2O2,
protecting cells from oxidative stress damage.
The enrichment of methanogenic genera capable of coping
with oxidative stress and the elevated abundance of antioxidant
enzyme genes might explain why methanogenesis could
proceed effectively under intermittent microaeration condi-
tions. This confirmed that the ability of anaerobic sludge to
cope with oxidative stress could be domesticated by O2
induction within the anaerobic digestion system, which is
consistent with the previous studies.62,63
Furthermore, in iron-containing anaerobic digestion sys-
tems, intermittent microaeration might oxidize Fe(II) to drive
the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle, which could enrich DIR bacterial and
enhance EET capacity. This mechanism preferentially directs
O2 reduction in the extracellular space to form extracellular
ROS, accelerating the degradation of the substrate and thus
minimizing the generation of intracellular ROS and its
associated detrimental effects. Reducing the permeability of
O2 into cells can alleviate the oxidative stress induced by it and
enhance O2 tolerance of anaerobic microorganisms.64
4. IMPLICATIONS
It has been reported that phenol with a concentration
exceeding 2000 mg/L can inhibit biological processes,
including anaerobic digestion, due to the toxic accumulation
of phenol.6,7 Therefore, pretreatment is a necessary step before
the biological treatment of phenolic wastewater. This study
demonstrated that the Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle and ROS
generation induced by intermittent microaeration significantly
enhanced phenol degradation. These findings suggested the
potential to reduce or even eliminate conventional pretreat-
ment processes, thus reducing the operational costs of
anaerobic treatment systems.
A recent study has reported the generation of ROS in
activated sludge systems,23 however, the influence of ROS
generation on anaerobic digestion and methanogenesis
remains unclear. This study investigated the ROS generation
induced by microaeration in anaerobic digestion and its
promotion of anaerobic performance. The intracellular ROS
scavenging mechanism enabled methanogens to survive under
intermittent microaeration. In addition, changes in the redox
potential of the environment can affect the distribution of
intracellular and extracellular ROS, as well as the redox state of
the cell, thereby regulating the associated metabolic
processes.62 Therefore, the adaptation of methanogens to

Furthermore, it should be noted that iron is a commonly
used additive in pretreatment or advanced treatment processes
within wastewater treatment systems.65,66 In these treatment
systems, microaeration of the anaerobic methanogenic or
hydrolytic acidification units was expected to improve
treatment efficiency and enhance the degradation of bio-
logically refractory substances.13,15 However, the reasons were
generally attributed to the enhancement of microbial
community diversity, and there is a lack of explanations from
the perspective of intrinsic mechanisms. This study provided a
new perspective for improving anaerobic systems with
intermittent microaeration and an effective method with
economic feasibility for upgrading existing wastewater treat-
ment systems (Text S5). This might also explain the enhanced
decomposition of pollutants in artificial and natural biofilm
systems in terms of chemical mechanisms, i.e., O2 gradient
results in an anaerobic environment inside the biofilm and
aerobic environment outside the biofilm, which could
potentially accelerate pollutant decomposition through the
generation of ROS via Fenton-like reactions.23 This hypothesis
requires further investigation.
